note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · GIANT MARSH GRASS
tiles.details: Find a tall coarse emergent marsh grass with broad serrulate blades and open 30–60 cm flowering panicle. Existing Florida head and habitat panels (0,1) plus real whole wetland growth (3) show habit. Texas Anahuac panel 5 shows ACTUAL joined basal shoots and fibrous rootlike material, but NOT an exposed underground rhizome or a Hays voucher. Culms ~2–3 m and rhizomatous habit are published descriptions, not measurements from these images.
tiles.short: Broad sharp-edged leaves and a large open wetland panicle

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE LONG LIGULE
tiles.details: The true eciliate membrane is on the inner blade/sheath junction, not the external node shown in panel 3. Published Kew measurement 6–20 mm. No current image proves the opened ligule with a ruler.
tiles.short: Open the collar: look for a 6–20 mm papery membrane

tiles.heading: 03 · MALE AND FEMALE
tiles.details: TRUE new organ evidence: gallery panel 7 (zero-based) shows orange EXSERTED ANTHERS on a source-identified Dallas flowering branch; panel 6 shows attached Texas branchlet spikelets, but does not resolve each spikelet's sex. Panel 4 has pale feathery floral parts whose exact stigma identity is not certified. Male anthers and female stigmas/fruits must be documented together on ONE vouchered branch at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler before mapping sex position. Modern Kew/USGS/NOAA place male toward branch bases and female toward tips; an older description reverses it. Do NOT arrow unverified female organs or infer sex from branch location. Published individual spikelets ~6–8 mm; glumes absent or obscure in modern Kew.
tiles.short: Both sexes occur on the same branch—identify the organs first
tiles.status: REAL ANTHERS PHOTOGRAPHED — FEMALE SPIKELET/SEX POSITION UNVERIFIED

tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA, AWN AND LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Kew reports female lemma 6–8 mm, seven-veined, with one 2–3 mm awn; male lemma awnless. Require actual 10–20× dissections with scale, then distinguish Phragmites's many-flowered silky plume, Arundo's plume, Tripsacum's jointed spike, and Leersia's smaller rice-like spikelets. Do not disturb endangered Zizania texana.
tiles.short: Female short-awned lemma; male lemma awnless

tiles.heading: 05 · LEAF TEETH AND BASE
tiles.details: Follow broad ~8–22-mm blades down to a tall reedlike culm. Existing panel 2 documents a real exterior sheath/node, NOT the opened long inner ligule. New Anahuac Texas panel 5 demonstrates joined basal shoots, old sheaths and rootlike fibers, NOT a photographed underground connecting rhizome. Leaf edges are reported serrulate; a 10–20× 1-mm-scaled image of actual margin teeth is still missing. Avoid sliding bare fingers along the blade or destructively collecting sensitive marsh plants.
tiles.short: Find sharp blade edges on a connected rhizomatous culm
tiles.status: REAL BASAL CROWN PHOTO — RHIZOME/MARGIN TEETH STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · REED OR CUTGRASS?
tiles.details: Use real giant-cutgrass open panicle (panel 0) and clearly DIFFERENT-SPECIES look-alike panels: Arundo donax (8), Phragmites australis of unresolved lineage (9), and protected Texas wild-rice Zizania texana (10). Phragmites/Arundo have silky multi-flowered plume spikelets; Zizaniopsis has separate one-flowered male and female spikelets, with real male anthers in target panel 7 but no same-branch confirmed female organs yet. Tripsacum dactyloides has jointed spikes with male units above female hard joints; Leersia oryzoides is smaller. Published Zizaniopsis female lemma ~6–8 mm with ~2–3 mm awn; male lemma awnless. Do not arrow unverified reproductive sex, label Phragmites lineage from habit, or disturb endangered Zizania texana.
tiles.short: Check real florets before calling a tall marsh grass
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE PANELS INSTALLED — SEX-CONFIRMED SPIKELET DISSECTION MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: GIANT CUTGRASS: look for a TALL coarse rhizomatous emergent marsh grass, broad saw-edged blades and an unusually large open to drooping many-branched panicle. Its separate MALE and FEMALE one-flowered spikelets occur on the SAME panicle branches; modern Kew and USGS/NOAA treatments place MALE spikelets BASAL and FEMALE spikelets toward branch tips, but older botanical descriptions REVERSE the positions. Confirm male anthers versus female stigma/fruit before applying any position-based rule; do not identify sex from head silhouette. Find the true LONG papery MEMBRANOUS ligule at a fresh blade–sheath junction, Kew usually 6–20 mm — not a tiny hair fringe. Confirm actual sex characters/spikelets with hand lens and mm scale. One Florida source photograph documents flowering-head form, not a Hays locality voucher.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with EIGHT archived exact-source giant cutgrass JPEGs: Florida flowering head and wetland habit, Texas joined basal shoots, Dallas attached panicle branches and actual orange ANTHERS. None establishes a Hays County voucher; the Anahuac crown does not expose underground rhizomes.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The true eciliate membrane is on the inner blade/sheath junction, not the external node shown in panel 3. Published Kew measurement 6–20 mm. No current image proves the opened ligule with a ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew reports female lemma 6–8 mm, seven-veined, with one 2–3 mm awn; male lemma awnless. Require actual 10–20× dissections with scale, then distinguish Phragmites's many-flowered silky plume, Arundo's plume, Tripsacum's jointed spike, and Leersia's smaller rice-like spikelets. Do not disturb endangered Zizania texana.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Giant cutgrass Zizaniopsis has tall coarse marsh growth; BROAD sharp-serrulate blades; a great loose 30–60-cm panicle with distinct separate one-flowered MALE and FEMALE spikelets on each branch (male basal/female terminal in modern treatments; historical accounts conflict, so verify actual sexual organs); and an unusually LONG membranous 6–20-mm ligule. Phragmites australis can have a distinctly feathery soft panicle; includes Texas native and introduced lineages, so a single morphology photograph does not certify invasion status. Introduced Arundo donax has a robust fluffy plume, bamboo-like cane and different spikelet/ligule details. Leersia oryzoides is generally smaller and has much smaller flattened narrow rice-shaped spikelets and tiny backward-pointing leaf teeth. Protected Zizania texana is aquatic wild-rice endemic to the San Marcos River and must not be handled for photographs. Tripsacum's thick single flowering spikes carry male units ABOVE female bead-like joints, opposite the mixed sex positions along Zizaniopsis panicle branches. Use paired reproductive/ligule photos before final call.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 1 · Open flowering panicle — actual Florida source photo
panels.caption: Original Alex Abair CC BY 4.0 photo examined: long upright green panicle held before a wetland boardwalk, with narrow branching seedhead divisions visible. A wide green grass blade is visible nearby; this image does NOT establish its attachment to the held inflorescence. Neither sexes, tiny glumes, true ligule nor serrulate teeth can be labelled individually.
panels.creator: Alex Abair

panels.label: 2 · Wild wetland growth, broad arching blades
panels.caption: The source-photo identified giant cutgrass clump shows long arching green blades rising from dense vegetation in open marsh. Underground rhizomes and a complete flowering stalk are NOT exposed.
panels.creator: Alex Abair

panels.label: 3 · Stem node and real leaf–sheath junction
panels.caption: The archived photo shows a swollen culm node higher on the stem and a grass blade leaving its lower enclosing sheath. The 6–20-mm membranous ligule is INSIDE this junction and not independently exposed or measured in this photograph. Minute margin teeth cannot be measured.

panels.label: WHOLE PLANT · wetland flowering growth next to a standing person for scale
panels.caption: Alex Abair’s Florida original documents a flowering giant cutgrass shoot beside a person, with large arching leaf blades and tall seed-bearing branches visibly emerging from the marsh vegetation. Use the person as gross scale only; no precise height, rhizome or true ligule is shown.
panels.creator: Alex Abair

panels.label: REAL REPRODUCTIVE MACRO · spikelet clusters and pale feathery floral parts
panels.caption: Alex Abair’s exact-species macro shows many narrow green spikelet-like units together with protruding pale feathery reproductive structures. These are REAL botanical parts attached to the panicle, not illustrations. Male/female floral sex, anther versus stigma attachment and glume/lemma differentiation are not reliably resolved; do not label sex or length here.
panels.creator: Alex Abair
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE · invasive giant reed (*Arundo donax*), tall broad-leaved dense canes
panels.caption: Arundo donax is a problematic exotic giant reed with tough thick upright cane-like culms, broad clasping blades, and a large fluffy panicle. Giant cutgrass is a marsh grass with different narrow rice-like spikelets including separate staminate/pistillate units; check flowering structure, not height alone. Avoid calling the stand here Zizaniopsis.
panels.creator: Forest & Kim Starr
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

memory_rule: BIG MARSH GRASS + 30–60 cm OPEN PANICLE + LONG 6–20 mm PAPERY LIGULE + separate MALE/FEMALE one-flowered spikelets on SAME branch. Modern sources place males basal, females terminal; historical sources reverse them. Confirm actual sexual organs before using position.
safety_note: Eight source-labelled species JPEGs are physically archived: original CC BY 4.0 photographs plus individually CC BY-NC 4.0 Texas basal/branch images. Existing 11 panels include 3 clearly different-species comparisons. Male anthers are actually visible, but the female spikelet, opened 6–20-mm ligule, 2–3-mm female awn insertion, leaf teeth and underground rhizome remain unverified. Modern/historical sex-position conflict is a SCIENTIFIC HOLD. No new photos/arrows or Pages verification in this finalization.
field_rule: 6–20 mm true membranous ligule + saw-edged wide blades + very large open wetland panicle + documented unisexual spikelets; genital position needs voucher-paired photos due historical-treatment discrepancy.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
